headline: World Concludes Anything Not Working Is Definitely a Cyberattack
subheadline: *Burnt toast, jammed printers and one man's unresponsive cat all reclassified as 'probable state-sponsored activity' following 24 hours of outages.*
author: Nigel Featherstone, Cybersecurity Panic Desk
seoTitle: World Blames Cyberattack for Everything Broken | The Daily Absurd
seoDescription: Satire: after Microsoft outages and grounded flights, humanity decides every broken thing — from toasters to marriages — is the work of shadowy hackers.
sourceEvent: A cluster of disruptions — tech stock turbulence, prolonged Microsoft outages and a nationwide grounding of flights — left the public asking whether interconnected systems were under cyberattack, with officials unable to immediately rule anything out. The events coincided with a global Microsoft 365 outage that disrupted email and workplace tools for roughly a day.

social.x: BREAKING: After 24 hours of outages, humanity has determined that everything currently broken — including your printer, your sourdough and Kevin's marriage — is a cyberattack. Investigators ask it to try turning itself off and on again.
social.facebook: Microsoft went down, the planes stopped flying, and within 24 hours the entire species agreed: nothing merely 'breaks' anymore. Your toaster is now a person of interest. Full report from our Cybersecurity Panic Desk.
social.linkedin: New research finds that after one day of outages, 100% of humans attribute any malfunction to a shadowy hacker collective. The sole mitigation strategy identified: asking the affected system if it has tried restarting.
social.instagram: The flight board says 'cyberattack', the coffee machine says 'cyberattack', and honestly at this point so does my left knee. #satire #cyberattack #techoutage
altHeadlines: Nation's Toasters Placed on Terror Watchlist Pending Investigation
Airlines Admit Entire Contingency Plan Is 'Unplug It and Count to Thirty'

body:
After 24 hours of Microsoft outages, grounded flights and general technological sulking, humanity reached a unanimous conclusion on Saturday: anything that has stopped working, anywhere, for any reason, is now officially a cyberattack.

The consensus formed within hours of a nationwide ground stop that left thousands of passengers stranded, which experts agreed could only plausibly be the work of a shadowy hacker collective, probably called something like 'Midnight Badger' or 'Lazarus-adjacent'.

"We are treating every malfunction as hostile until proven otherwise," said a spokesperson for an unnamed national cybersecurity agency. "This includes the vending machine on level three, which has refused a two-pound coin for the third time this week and is therefore considered a person of interest."

By midday, the theory had expanded well beyond aviation and email. Burnt toast was reclassified as an intrusion. A jammed printer in a Leeds council office was declared 'a textbook advanced persistent threat'. One local man reported his cat had been ignoring him since Thursday, which he described as 'almost certainly foreign interference'.

"The pattern is unmistakable," said one analyst, gesturing at a corkboard covered in red string. "Things were working, and then they stopped. That is exactly what a cyberattack looks like. It is also what Tuesday looks like, but we are not taking chances."

In response, the world activated its single known cybersecurity protocol: asking the broken thing whether it has tried turning itself off and on again. The United Nations convened an emergency session at which delegates formally requested that the global technology stack 'hold the power button down for ten seconds'. The stack did not respond, which officials called 'deeply suspicious' and 'precisely what it would want us to think'.

Airports have since begun rebooting aircraft on a rolling basis. One major airline admitted its entire business continuity plan is a laminated card reading 'unplug it, count to thirty', while another announced it had 'turned the sky off and back on' with mixed results.

Meanwhile, a couple in Manchester has paused divorce proceedings while investigators determine whether the marriage was compromised by the same threat actor believed responsible for a slow-loading spreadsheet.

At press time, investigators confirmed the outages had been caused by a routine configuration error — prompting the public to conclude that the configuration error had itself been hacked.
